title: Wedding at Cana
note: Core lesson: when we have a problem or are worried, we can tell Jesus, because he cares for us and can help us. The chapter's decision, and the line it lands on, is “I will tell Jesus everything.” Three acts, as Chapter 1: Connect — the modern child and Story Halo, a worry the child already knows; Discover — Cana itself, Story Halo absent; Reflect — back to the child, Story Halo returns. The panel sequence and every line of dialogue are pending approval and are deliberately not written down here: a numbered list of events sitting in this file would be read as a storyboard, and this chapter does not have one yet. Jesus and Mary are recurring characters — face, age, hair, skin, proportions and rendering language stay as Chapter 1 established them, and only clothing, pose and composition change.

cover.note: Pending. Drawn once the storyboard is approved. Chapter 1 paints the chapter title into the cover artwork itself and this one should too — the reader lays no text over a cover.

story.alt: A boy sits at his desk with his chin in his hands, looking worried. Above him the question reads, “What do you do when you are worried or have a problem?”, with three small pictures — a difficult test, a problem with a friend, and something that gets broken. Halo glows beside him and says, “You can tell Jesus about it! He always listens and cares.”
story.note: Act 1, Connect. The chapter opens on the child's own worry before it opens on the Bible, and the three small pictures are there so a six-year-old finds their own kind of problem in one of them.

story.alt: Halo says, “Someone in the Bible had a problem too.” A thought bubble above the boy shows Jesus and Mary at a wedding feast. The boy asks, “Really? What happened?”
story.note: Act 1. The bridge: the child's problem and the Bible's problem are the same kind of thing.

story.alt: The boy lies on his bed with a big storybook open in front of him. Halo says, “Let’s find out what happened!” and the picture above shows the wedding at Cana, with the words, “Jesus, his mother Mary, and his disciples were invited to a wedding in Cana.”
story.note: Act 1 ends here, on the way in. The next panel is inside the story.

story.alt: Jesus and his mother Mary walk with his disciples through a flowered archway. A sign reads, “Welcome to the Wedding in Cana.” The words above say, “Jesus, his mother Mary, and his disciples were invited to a wedding in Cana.”
story.note: Act 2, Discover, begins. Halo is absent from every panel from here to panel-14, which is the rule and not an oversight.

story.alt: A long table full of food and flowers, with musicians and guests all around. Jesus and Mary sit together among them. The words say, “The wedding was a happy celebration. Everyone was enjoying the feast!”
A servant holds an empty jar and another spreads his hands, both worried. Empty cups stand on the table. The words say, “But during the feast, the wine ran out.”

Mary stands behind a pillar, listening, while three servants talk beside the six stone jars. One says, “The wine has run out!” and another says, “What can we do now?” The words say, “Mary overheard the servants talking about the problem.”
story.note: The first panel where all six stone jars are in shot.

story.alt: Mary leans towards Jesus with her hand on her chest and says, “They have no wine.” Jesus listens. The words say, “Mary went to Jesus and told him about the problem.”
story.note: The heart of the chapter, and the thing the lesson is about: somebody noticed a problem and took it to Jesus. The reader's one question asks about this panel.

story.alt: Mary turns to the servants by the stone jars and says, “If he commands you to do anything, do it.” The words say, “Mary told the servants to do whatever Jesus said.”
Jesus points towards the stone jars and says, “Fill the jars with water,” while the servants begin to pour. The words say, “Jesus told the servants what to do.”
The servants pour water from smaller jugs into the six big stone jars, and the water shines as it falls. The words say, “The servants filled the six stone jars with water.”
The water in the six stone jars has turned deep red. The servants and Mary look at it in astonishment. The words say, “The water became wine!”
A servant lifts a golden cup, delighted, and says, “It’s wine! Wonderful wine!” The words say, “The servants tasted the water, and it was wine!”

Jesus raises a cup among the smiling guests and one of them says, “This is amazing!” The words say, “Jesus did his first miracle at the wedding in Cana. He showed his glory, and his disciples believed in him.” The reference below reads John 2:11.
story.note: Act 2 closes on the miracle being named as the first one. Halo returns on the next panel.

story.alt: The boy is back at his desk at home, resting his chin on his hand. Halo glows beside him and asks, “Do you ever have problems that make you worried or sad?”
story.note: Act 3, Reflect. The same room and the same pose as panel-01, on purpose — the child is being asked their own question back, now that they know the story.

story.alt: The boy looks up, easier now, and Halo says, “Jesus cares about you. You can tell Him everything.”

The boy kneels by his bed with his hands folded and his eyes closed, Halo glowing beside him. A card reads, “My decision: I will tell Jesus everything,” and beneath it, 1 Peter 5:7 — “Cast all your anxiety on him, because he cares for you.”
story.note: My Decision, and the memory verse, both painted into the artwork — the same shape Chapter 1 uses, where the chapter lands on the child's own answer rather than on a summary. There is no separate decision screen because there has never been one.

games.title: Fill the Six Jars
games.objective: Do what the servants did — fill all six stone jars, and see what Jesus does with the water.
games.note: The chapter's own game, and the one that is not a question. A child can be asked what Jesus told the servants to do and pick the right word out of three; or they can fill the jars. Six items because the story says six, and nothing here can be got wrong — see the reveal note in the schema.

games.title: The Day at Cana
games.objective: Put the day back in order, from the feast to the miracle.
games.note: Each step is the panel that draws it: the feast, the wine running out, Mary telling Jesus, the jars being filled, the water turned. A child who has just read the story is putting the pictures back in order rather than reading five sentences and sorting them, which is the difference between remembering a story and parsing a list. The labels stay for whoever cannot see the pictures.

interactions.hint: The wedding had only just begun.

games.title: What Do You Remember?
games.objective: Recall the facts of the miracle: the town, what ran out, the six jars, and what the water became.

interactions.hint: It was a little town called Cana.

interactions.prompt: What ran out at the wedding?
interactions.hint: There was not enough left to drink.

interactions.prompt: How many stone jars were there?
What did Jesus say to fill them with?
interactions.hint: You draw it from a well.
It was the thing that had run out.

interactions.prompt: What was special about this miracle?
interactions.hint: Jesus had never done one before this day.

games.note: Shelf picture: The moment the game is mostly about: six jars of water gone deep red.

games.title: Right or Wrong?
games.objective: Tell what really happened at Cana from what did not.
games.note: True-and-false, built from the presentations that exist rather than as a sixth one: the statement is the prompt and the two answers are the choices. Three of the five statements were reworded — the curriculum's wording runs past the ten-word prompt limit and uses words like “informed”, which a six-year-old reads over. The meaning of each, and whether it is right or wrong, is unchanged. Shelf picture: Mary listening to the servants beside the jars — the problem being noticed, which is what most of these statements circle.

interactions.prompt: Jesus was not invited to the wedding.
interactions.hint: He was there with his mother and his friends.

interactions.prompt: The wine ran out at the wedding.
interactions.hint: That was the problem Mary noticed.

interactions.prompt: Mary told Jesus about the problem.
interactions.hint: She noticed first, and she went straight to him.
Count again — it was one more than five.
It was the very first one he ever did.

quiz.prompt: Who told Jesus about the problem?
quiz.note: One question, in the reader, where Chapter 1 puts one: a gentle “did you notice?” between the last panel and the ending, not a test. It asks the thing the chapter is about — that somebody noticed a problem and took it to Jesus — and the rest of the recall lives in the games, which is where a child chooses to go.

verse.text: Cast all your anxiety on him, because he cares for you.

practice.hint: It begins with what you do with your worries.

verse.note: Supplied with the chapter. The translation is deliberately unresolved: this wording is not the World English Bible's, which is the public-domain text Chapter 1 uses, so which translation is credited — and whether it may be used — is still open. PLACEHOLDER is what keeps that from being decided by accident; checks.ts warns while the chapter is a draft and refuses it once the chapter is listed in library.json.

celebration.message: You learned how Mary told Jesus, and how He helped.
celebration.note: A recap, because the decision now has its own place. This field held “I will tell Jesus everything.” while the storyboard was pending, and panel-17 turned out to paint that line into the artwork itself, under the words “My decision”. Saying it again one page later would take the child's own moment and repeat it back as a caption.
